title: Don't Waste Population: Post-Anneal Refinement for Combinatorial Optimization
claim: Baselines refine only the single best candidate and stay in one basin; ours uses diverse candidates and paths to reach a better optimum.
layout: 2 stacked panels (A baseline, B ours), shared landscape motif, candidate color bars at left
description: Two vertically stacked panels share the same schematic contour landscape of basins, drawn as a pale blue blob with shaded wells. Panel A, Baseline, has a column of candidate bars on the left. One solid blue bar is used and the other five are gray hatched and labeled 'Unused candidates'. On the landscape, a blue dot is polished by a downward arrow to a blue star in a shallow basin. Panel B, I-PRP, has six bars: five colored and labeled Top-K candidates, plus one hatched. On the landscape, a blue star sends dashed 'Relink' paths with waypoints to green stars. A purple diamond on one path is polished again, shown by an orange arrow, into a large orange star in the deepest basin, labeled 'Better solution'. The eye goes first to the bold panel titles, then to the colored stars.
caption: Post-anneal refinement. (A) The baseline polishes only the best rounded replica. (B) I-PRP polishes the top-K elites and follows separate paths from the best polished elite to the others. Re- polishing an intermediate state can reach a better basin. The paths retain their endpoints throughout each pass; the landscape is schematic.
abstract: Parallel annealers generate diverse candidate solutions; yet, conventional post-processing typically refines only the best, leaving much of the population's potential untapped. We introduce Iterative Path-Relinking Polish (I-PRP), a deterministic, training-free method that exploits this diversity to discover better solutions without modifying the underlying annealing process. I-PRP selects promising candidates, explores cost-guided paths between locally optimized solutions, and refines intermediate states to uncover better local minima. Newly discovered improvements are iteratively incorporated into the population, enabling further exploration. We theoretically guarantee that I-PRP never degrades solution quality relative to conventional single-candidate polishing on the same population and converges in finitely many iterations. Experiments across challenging combinatorial optimization benchmarks, including MaxCut, MaxClique, and graph coloring, demonstrate substantial improvements in several instances. Paired evaluations confirm non-degradation, while matched-runtime comparisons show that exploiting existing population diversity can outperform additional annealing. These results establish I-PRP as an effective and reliable refinement strategy for parallel annealing.
